claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to medical literature.

claims.claim: Drosophila larvae provide a useful model system for the studies of feeding behavior and nutrition intake.
claims.source: Drosophila larvae provide a useful model system for the studies of feeding behavior and nutrition intake (Ikeya et al., 2002; Rulifson et al., 2002; Hwangbo et al., 2004; Bader et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: In Caenorhabditis elegans two groups of excitatory GABAergic motor neurons have been identified with partially redundant functions in activating enteric muscle cells (EMCs).
claims.source: In Caenorhabditis elegans two groups of excitatory GABAergic motor neurons have been identified with partially redundant functions in activating enteric muscle cells (EMCs) (McIntire et al., 1993).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work in C. elegans.

claims.claim: The Drosophila larval hindgut is the last part of the intestine, posterior to the Malpighian tubule, on the dorsal side under larval cuticle.
claims.source: The Drosophila larval hindgut is the last part of the intestine, posterior to the Malpighian tubule, on the dorsal side under larval cuticle.
claims.evidence: This is an anatomical description supported by the figures.

claims.claim: The anal sphincter has a layer of thick sphincter muscles and a much narrower canal.
claims.source: At the posterior end of the hindgut is anal sphincter, which has a layer of thick sphincter muscles and a much narrower canal (Figure 1A, Figure1—figure supplement 1) (Murakami and Shiotsuki, 2001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by anatomical observations and citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: The defecation process is repeated every 38 s at 25°C.
claims.source: This defecation process is repeated every 38 s at 25°C (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: PDF neurons and HGN1 neurons have their cell bodies in the terminal segments of VNC.
claims.source: These neurons have their cell bodies in the terminal segments of VNC (Figure 1E) and send their axons along the midline of the ventral body wall to the posterior end of the larva, where they enter the hindgut.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by anatomical imaging shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: HGN1 axons extend posteriorly to the anus sphincter surface to form dense arborizations over the muscles.
claims.source: Within the hindgut, the HGN1 axons extend posteriorly to the anus sphincter surface to form dense arborizations over the muscles, while the PDF axons arborize over the posterior two-third of the hindgut with refined branches (Figure 1F–H).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by anatomical imaging shown in Figure 1F-H.

claims.claim: PDF axons arborize over the posterior two-third of the hindgut with refined branches.
claims.source: Within the hindgut, the HGN1 axons extend posteriorly to the anus sphincter surface to form dense arborizations over the muscles, while the PDF axons arborize over the posterior two-third of the hindgut with refined branches (Figure 1F–H).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by anatomical imaging shown in Figure 1F-H.

claims.claim: PDF and HGN1 neurons are glutamatergic.
claims.source: The PDF and HGN1 neurons are glutamatergic, as they could be labeled with antibody staining against Drosophila vGlut (Daniels et al., 2008) (Figure 1K,L).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining experiments shown in Figure 1K,L.

claims.claim: Illumination of the larval VNC with blue light caused a dramatic increase of EJPs in the anus sphincter muscles in the larva with ChR2 expression in the HGN1 neurons.
claims.source: Illumination of the larval VNC with blue light caused a dramatic increase of EJPs in the anus sphincter muscles in the larva with ChR2 expression in the HGN1 neurons but not in the control animals (Figure 2B,C), providing evidence for HGN1 innervation of sphincter muscles.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2B,C.

claims.claim: Activation of PDF neurons expressing ChR2 with blue light triggered a dramatic increase of EJPs in the anus sphincter muscles.
claims.source: Activation of PDF neurons expressing ChR2 with blue light also triggered a dramatic increase of EJPs in the anus sphincter muscles (Figure 2B,C), indicating that PDF neurons also play a role in regulating anal sphincter contractions, although PDF neurons do not directly form synapse with these muscles.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2B,C.

claims.claim: PDF neurons do not directly form synapse with anal sphincter muscles.
claims.source: Activation of PDF neurons expressing ChR2 with blue light also triggered a dramatic increase of EJPs in the anus sphincter muscles (Figure 2B,C), indicating that PDF neurons also play a role in regulating anal sphincter contractions, although PDF neurons do not directly form synapse with these muscles.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the anatomical observations showing PDF axons do not directly innervate the anal sphincter.

claims.claim: Silencing PDF neurons caused the interval of the defecation to increase from 38 s to 94 s.
claims.source: Silencing PDF neurons caused the interval of the defecation to increase from 38 s to 94 s (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral experiments using Kir2.1 to silence neurons, shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Silencing the HGN1 neurons did not significantly alter the interval of anus sphincter opening.
claims.source: Silencing the HGN1 neurons did not significantly alter the interval of anus sphincter opening (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Silencing both the PDF neurons and HGN1 neurons caused the larva to display barely any hindgut movement over 5 min.
claims.source: Indeed, silencing both the PDF neurons and HGN1 neurons caused the larva to display barely any hindgut movement over 5 min thus rendering it difficult to estimate the defecation interval, in contrast to the nearly eight cycles of contraction over 5 min—corresponding to a defecation interval of 38 s—in control animals (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: PDF neurons displayed a stereotypical periodic firing pattern with an average interval between peak Ca2+ signals of 38 s.
claims.source: Indeed, the PDF neurons displayed a stereotypical periodic firing pattern as revealed by Ca2+ elevation in both soma and dendrite area (Figure 4A,C). The average interval between peak Ca2+ signals is 38 s, which is highly consistent with the temporal pattern of contraction of the hindgut (Figure 1D and Figure 4M).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 4A,C,M.

claims.claim: HGN1 neurons exhibited oscillation of Ca2+ levels with a periodicity of 38 s.
claims.source: We also monitored the Ca2+ signals of the HGN1 neurons and found that the HGN1 neurons also exhibited oscillation of Ca2+ levels with a periodicity of 38 s (Figure 4B,D,M, Video 3).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 4B,D,M.

claims.claim: Ca2+ signals of HGN1 neurons spread from dendrites to soma with a fixed latency.
claims.source: Furthermore, Ca2+ signals of HGN1 neurons spread from dendrites to soma with a fixed latency (Video 3), indicating that the HGN1 neurons may receive excitatory inputs with a periodicity of 38 s.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging shown in Video 3.

claims.claim: HGN1 neurons may receive excitatory inputs with a periodicity of 38 s.
claims.source: Furthermore, Ca2+ signals of HGN1 neurons spread from dendrites to soma with a fixed latency (Video 3), indicating that the HGN1 neurons may receive excitatory inputs with a periodicity of 38 s.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of calcium signal propagation.

claims.claim: The arborizations of PDF neurons and HGN1 neurons overlap extensively along the midline of the posterior VNC.
claims.source: The arborizations of PDF neurons and HGN1 neurons overlap extensively along the midline of the posterior VNC (Figure 4E,F and Video 4), raising the question whether they interact with each other.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by anatomical imaging shown in Figure 4E,F and Video 4.

claims.claim: An intense GFP signal was observed in the area where the processes of PDF and HGN1 neurons overlap using GRASP.
claims.source: We expressed the two GFP components separately in PDF neurons and HGN1 neurons by using two different binary expression systems, PDF-LexA and HGN1-Gal4. An intense GFP signal was observed in the area where the processes of these two groups of neurons overlap (Figure 4G), while neither PDF neuron nor HGN1 neuron expressing one part of the split GFP of GRASP generated any fluorescent signals by itself (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), suggesting that a functional connection might exist between PDF and HGN1 neurons.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by GRASP experiments shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: A functional connection might exist between PDF and HGN1 neurons.
claims.source: We expressed the two GFP components separately in PDF neurons and HGN1 neurons by using two different binary expression systems, PDF-LexA and HGN1-Gal4. An intense GFP signal was observed in the area where the processes of these two groups of neurons overlap (Figure 4G), while neither PDF neuron nor HGN1 neuron expressing one part of the split GFP of GRASP generated any fluorescent signals by itself (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), suggesting that a functional connection might exist between PDF and HGN1 neurons.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from GRASP results indicating close proximity of neuronal processes.

claims.claim: PDF neurons send their axons to the area where their processes overlap with HGN1 neuron dendrites.
claims.source: By labeling the PDF neurons simultaneously with the dendritic RFP marker DenMark and the axonal GFP marker sytGFP, we found that the PDF neurons send their axons to the area where their processes overlap with HGN1 neuron dendrites (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by dual labeling experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: The Ca2+ level began to rise in PDF neuron cell bodies and then spread to the area occupied by arborizations of both groups of neurons, followed by Ca2+ elevation in the cell bodies of HGN1 neurons with a very short delay.
claims.source: By monitoring the Ca2+ signals in PDF neurons and HGN1 neurons simultaneously, we found that the Ca2+ level began to rise in PDF neuron cell bodies and then spread to the area occupied by arborizations of both groups of neurons, followed by Ca2+ elevation in the cell bodies of HGN1 neurons with a very short delay, indicating that these two groups of neurons have coordinated firing patterns (Figure 4H–L and Video 5).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by simultaneous calcium imaging shown in Figure 4H-L and Video 5.

claims.claim: PDF neurons and HGN1 neurons have coordinated firing patterns.
claims.source: By monitoring the Ca2+ signals in PDF neurons and HGN1 neurons simultaneously, we found that the Ca2+ level began to rise in PDF neuron cell bodies and then spread to the area occupied by arborizations of both groups of neurons, followed by Ca2+ elevation in the cell bodies of HGN1 neurons with a very short delay, indicating that these two groups of neurons have coordinated firing patterns (Figure 4H–L and Video 5).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the sequential calcium signals observed in the two neuronal groups.

claims.claim: A specialized PPK-Gal4-labeled neuron was found in the vicinity of the anal slit.
claims.source: In the vicinity of the anal slit, we found a specialized PPK-Gal4-labeled neuron.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by anatomical characterization using PPK-Gal4 driver.

claims.claim: The cell body of the anus sensory neuron resides on the anterior side of the anal slit, and its dendritic arbors surround the entire anal slit.
claims.source: The cell body of this neuron resides on the anterior side of the anal slit, and its dendritic arbors surround the entire anal slit (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by anatomical imaging shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: The majority of ASN dendrites forms a thin layer of arbors and covers the body wall around the anal slit.
claims.source: The majority of its dendrites forms a thin layer of arbors and covers the body wall around the anal slit (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by anatomical imaging shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Some ASN arborizations extend along the anus sphincter.
claims.source: There are also some arborizations extending along the anus sphincter (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by anatomical imaging shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: The axon of the anus sensory neuron joins the nerve bundle that includes the axons of other da neurons and projects to the terminal segment of the VNC.
claims.source: The axon of this sensory neuron joins the nerve bundle that includes the axons of other da neurons and projects to the terminal segment of the VNC.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by anatomical tracing.

claims.claim: When the anal slit opens, the ASN dendrites are dramatically stretched.
claims.source: When the anal slit opens, the dendrites are dramatically stretched (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Opening of the anal slit is accompanied with Ca2+ elevation in both dendrites and soma of the ASN.
claims.source: We found that opening of the anal slit is accompanied with Ca2+ elevation in both dendrites and soma of this neuron (Figure 5C,D and Video 6).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging shown in Figure 5C,D and Video 6.

claims.claim: The periodicity of ASN Ca2+ response is similar to that of the movements of the anus and the oscillations of PDF neurons and HGN1 neurons in the VNC.
claims.source: The periodicity of this Ca2+ response is similar to that of the movements of the anus and the oscillations of PDF neurons and HGN1 neurons in the VNC (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative comparison shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: The ASN is mechanosensitive and participates in sensing the radial stretch caused by opening the anus.
claims.source: This result indicates that the ASN is mechanosensitive and participates in sensing the radial stretch caused by opening the anus.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the calcium responses observed when the anus opens.

claims.claim: The ASN projects to the terminal segments of the VNC and its axon terminals overlap with the area occupied by the dendrites of the HGN1 neurons and PDF neurons.
claims.source: This sensory neuron projects to the terminal segments of the VNC and its axon terminals overlap with the area occupied by the dendrites of the HGN1 neurons and PDF neurons (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by anatomical imaging shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: There is very strong GRASP signal at the site where ASN axons and PDF dendrites overlap.
claims.source: We found that there is very strong GRASP signal at the site where ASN axons and PDF dendrites overlap (Figure 5G), while neither PDF neurons nor ASN expressing one part of the split GFP of GRASP generated any fluorescent signals (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by GRASP experiments shown in Figure 5G.

claims.claim: The GRASP signal between ASN and PDF neurons is asymmetric, in concordance with the localization of the ASN cell body to one side of the midline.
claims.source: Interestingly, the GRASP signal is asymmetric, in concordance with the localization of the ASN cell body to one side of the midline leading to a more intense axonal projection to the ipsilateral VNC, which is also evident with asymmetric Ca2+ elevation of the ASN axon terminals in the VNC (Video 7).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by GRASP imaging and calcium imaging shown in Video 7.

claims.claim: Activation of ASN via blue light illumination induced large increases of EJPs in the majority of the anus sphincter muscles.
claims.source: Activation of ASN via blue light illumination induced large increases of EJPs in the majority of the anus sphincter muscles (Figure 5H,I).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by optogenetic activation and electrophysiological recording shown in Figure 5H,I.

claims.claim: Both PDF and HGN1 neurons responded to mechanical stimulation of the anus with a glass probe.
claims.source: We found that both PDF and HGN1 neurons responded to this local stimulation (Figure 5J).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging during mechanical stimulation shown in Figure 5J.

claims.claim: Laser ablation of ASN at 48 hr AEL completely abolished the ASN 48 hr after ablation, while the other PPK neurons remained intact.
claims.source: The ASN was completely abolished 48 hr after laser ablation, while the other PPK neurons remained intact (Figure 5K).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging after laser ablation shown in Figure 5K.

claims.claim: After ASN ablation, HGN1 neurons displayed abnormality of their rhythmic firing pattern with a much longer interval compared to control animals.
claims.source: We then imaged the cell bodies of HGN1 neurons in the VNC and found abnormality of their rhythmic firing pattern, which displayed a much longer interval compared to control animals (Figure 5L).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging after ASN ablation shown in Figure 5L.

claims.claim: The sensory neuron in the anus might sense the stretch when the anal slit is open and respond by providing feedback modulation of the PDF neurons and HGN1 neurons in the central nervous system.
claims.source: These results suggest that the central neurons in the VNC receive excitatory feedback from ASN to increase motor neuron firing. Together with the GRASP analysis revealing the physical proximity of the processes of ASN and PDF neurons, our results indicate that the sensory neuron in the anus might sense the stretch when the anal slit is open and respond by provide feedback modulation of the PDF neurons and HGN1 neurons in the central nervous system.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the combination of anatomical, functional, and ablation experiments.

claims.claim: The defecation rhythm remains normal in the iav, nan, and piezo mutants.
claims.source: We found that the defecation rhythm remains normal in the iav, nan, and piezo mutants.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral measurements in mutant animals.

claims.claim: The defecation interval in the nompC mutants was significantly increased.
claims.source: However, the defecation interval in the nompC mutants was significantly increased (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by behavioral measurements shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: NOMPC is a TRPN channel essential for adult hearing and larval gentle touch.
claims.source: NOMPC is a TRPN channel essential for adult hearing and larval gentle touch (Gong et al., 2004; Yan et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: NOMPC is highly expressed all over the dendrites and soma of the ASN.
claims.source: We found that NOMPC is highly expressed all over the dendrites and soma of the ASN, as revealed by staining with antibody against the NOMPC protein (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), raising the possibility that it might play a role in ASN sensing of radial stretch.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The Ca2+ response is absent in the ASN of nompC null mutant larvae.
claims.source: Indeed, we found that the Ca2+ response is absent in the ASN of nompC null mutant larvae (Figure 6B,C, Video 8).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging in nompC mutants shown in Figure 6B,C and Video 8.

claims.claim: The defect in ASN Ca2+ response in nompC mutants could be rescued by expressing wild-type NOMPC in the ASN with PPK-Gal4.
claims.source: This defect could be rescued by expressing wild-type NOMPC in the ASN with PPK-Gal4 (Figure 6B,C, Video 9).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by rescue experiments shown in Figure 6B,C and Video 9.

claims.claim: The ASN of iav1 mutant larvae exhibited Ca2+ response comparable to that in the wild-type larvae.
claims.source: We found the ASN of iav1 mutant larvae exhibited Ca2+ response comparable to that in the wild-type larvae (Figure 6C and Video 10), suggesting that IAV is not required for the mechanotransduction of ASN.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging in iav mutants shown in Figure 6C and Video 10.

claims.claim: IAV is not required for the mechanotransduction of ASN.
claims.source: We found the ASN of iav1 mutant larvae exhibited Ca2+ response comparable to that in the wild-type larvae (Figure 6C and Video 10), suggesting that IAV is not required for the mechanotransduction of ASN.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the normal calcium responses in iav mutants.

claims.claim: Drosophila larvae exhibit rhythmic cycles of sequential contractions of the hindgut and the anal sphincter.
claims.source: We found that Drosophila larvae exhibit periodic defecation cycles, involving sequential contractions of the hindgut and the anal sphincter.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the behavioral observations throughout the study.

claims.claim: Two groups of neurons innervate the hindgut and anal sphincter respectively, and can excite the hindgut and anal sphincter muscle in a sequential manner.
claims.source: We also found two groups of neurons, which innervate the hindgut and anal sphincter respectively, and can excite the hindgut and anal sphincter muscle in a sequential manner.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the anatomical and functional characterization throughout the study.

claims.claim: A single sensory neuron could sense the opening of the anal slit and send feedback to the motor neurons.
claims.source: In addition, we found a single sensory neuron that could sense the opening of the anal slit and send feedback to the motor neurons (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the characterization of the ASN throughout the study.

claims.claim: At the larval stage, the motor neurons and gut muscles as well as the sensory neuron responding to anus movement, all show very robust rhythmic activities.
claims.source: However, at the larval stage, the motor neurons and gut muscles as well as the sensory neuron responding to anus movement, all show very robust rhythmic activities.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement based on the calcium imaging and behavioral observations.

claims.claim: Robust rhythmic feeding and defecation behaviors may facilitate larval nutrition intake and waste expulsion.
claims.source: Given that feeding and defecation are dominant behaviors for third-instar larvae, conceivably robust rhythmic feeding and defecation behaviors may facilitate their nutrition intake and waste expulsion.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed robust rhythmic behaviors.

claims.claim: Adult flies may need to conduct their defection behaviors in a more controllable manner due to encountering more complex environments.
claims.source: In contrast, adult flies will likely encounter more complex environments and may need to conduct their defection behaviors in a more controllable manner.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative comparison between larval and adult defecation behaviors.

claims.claim: The ASN could be labeled by both class III da neuronal marker and class IV da neuronal maker.
claims.source: Interestingly, the ASN could be labeled by both class III da neuronal marker and class IV da neuronal maker, raising the question whether it might have the dual functions to sense different stimuli.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an observation that raises a question for future investigation.

claims.claim: The two motor neurons appear to be functionally connected, possibly involving synaptic connections between them.
claims.source: The two motor neurons appear to be functionally connected, possibly involving synaptic connections between them, although we cannot exclude the possibility of multiple neurons being engaged in their functional connections.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the GRASP results and sequential firing patterns, but acknowledged as uncertain.

claims.claim: It remains to be determined as to how PDF and HGN1 neurons are entrained with this rhythmic firing pattern, and whether it involves a central pattern generator upstream of PDF neurons.
claims.source: It remains to be determined as to how they are entrained with this rhythmic firing pattern, and whether it involves a central pattern generator upstream of PDF neurons.
claims.evidence: This is stated as an open question for future research.

claims.claim: PDF is a peptide that has important roles in multiple neuropeptide signaling pathways in the fruit fly.
claims.source: Interestingly, PDF is a peptide that has important roles in multiple neuropeptide signaling pathways in the fruit fly (Renn et al., 1999; Kim et al., 2013); it would be interesting to test whether this neuropeptide also plays a role in the regulation of defecation behaviors by PDF neurons in the VNC.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: A recent study has suggested a novel role of HGN1 neurons in regulating the long-term food intake behaviors of adult flies.
claims.source: Recently, a study has suggested a novel role of HGN1 neurons in regulating the long-term food intake behaviors of adult flies (Olds and Xu, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claims.claim: HGN1 neurons control the rhythmic pattern of larval defecation.
claims.source: In our study we found that HGN1 neurons control the rhythmic pattern of larval defecation.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of findings from the current study.

claims.claim: Drosophila HGN1 neurons at different developmental stages might have multiple functions in regulating feeding and defecation behaviors.
claims.source: These two studies suggest that Drosophila HGN1 neurons at different developmental stages might have multiple functions in regulating feeding and defecation behaviors.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from comparing the current study with previous work on HGN1 neurons.

claims.claim: The structures of Drosophila gut and human gut share striking similarity.
claims.source: Though separated in evolution millions years ago, the structures of Drosophila gut and human gut share striking similarity.
claims.evidence: This is a general comparative statement based on anatomical knowledge.

claims.claim: There are circular and longitudinal muscles lining the gut ending with the anal sphincter that controls defecation in both Drosophila and humans.
claims.source: There are circular and longitudinal muscles lining the gut ending with the anal sphincter that controls defecation (Netter, 1997; Murakami and Shiotsuki, 2001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to anatomical references.

claims.claim: Diseases such as Hirschsprung's disease and anorectal malformation with failure to pass meconium are caused by developmental abnormality related to the gut and its innervation.
claims.source: Diseases such as Hirschsprung's disease and anorectal malformation with failure to pass meconium (Loening-Baucke and Kimura, 1999) are caused by developmental abnormality related to the gut and its innervation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to medical literature.

claims.claim: Mutations in two human genes could lead to the absence of certain nerve cells in the colon.
claims.source: Mutations in two human genes could lead to the absence of certain nerve cells in the colon (Puri and Shinkai, 2004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to medical literature.

claims.claim: The Drosophila larval body wall is transparent.
claims.source: Because the Drosophila larval body wall is transparent, contractions of the hindgut and anal sphincter can be monitored in vivo.
claims.evidence: This is a known property of Drosophila larvae that enables the experimental approach.

claims.claim: Contractions of the hindgut and anal sphincter can be monitored in vivo in Drosophila larvae.
claims.source: Because the Drosophila larval body wall is transparent, contractions of the hindgut and anal sphincter can be monitored in vivo.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental approach used throughout the study.

claims.claim: Each sequential contraction of hindgut and anus sphincter triggered a defecation cycle to expel feces out of the body.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 1C and Video 1, each sequential contraction of hindgut and anus sphincter triggered a defecation cycle to expel feces out of the body.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by video recordings shown in Figure 1C and Video 1.

claims.claim: The axons that innervate the hindgut are from the most posterior pair of the axon bundles in the ventral nerve cord (VNC).
claims.source: Since the axons that innervate the hindgut are from the most posterior pair of the axon bundles in the ventral nerve cord (VNC), the cell bodies of the neurons that innervate the hindgut and anal sphincter are most likely in the terminal segments of the VNC.
claims.evidence: This is based on anatomical tracing observations.

claims.claim: The cell bodies of the neurons that innervate the hindgut and anal sphincter are most likely in the terminal segments of the VNC.
claims.source: Since the axons that innervate the hindgut are from the most posterior pair of the axon bundles in the ventral nerve cord (VNC), the cell bodies of the neurons that innervate the hindgut and anal sphincter are most likely in the terminal segments of the VNC.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the anatomical organization of the nervous system.

claims.claim: PDF neurons and HGN1 neurons send their axons along the midline of the ventral body wall to the posterior end of the larva, where they enter the hindgut.
claims.source: These neurons have their cell bodies in the terminal segments of VNC (Figure 1E) and send their axons along the midline of the ventral body wall to the posterior end of the larva, where they enter the hindgut.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by anatomical tracing.

claims.claim: The labeled neurons in both PDF and HGN1 cases have their axon terminals in close proximity of the gut muscles and form abundant bouton structures.
claims.source: The labeled neurons in both cases have their axon terminals in close proximity of the gut muscles and form abundant bouton structures (Figure 1I,J).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by high-resolution imaging shown in Figure 1I,J.

claims.claim: PDF and HGN1 neurons are likely motor neurons that might play a role in regulating hindgut contractions.
claims.source: These results suggest that PDF and HGN1 neurons, which are likely motor neurons, might play a role in regulating hindgut contractions (Figure 1M).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the anatomical and molecular characterization showing glutamatergic identity and innervation of gut muscles.

claims.claim: The gut muscles received tonic excitatory inputs.
claims.source: The gut muscles received tonic excitatory inputs (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: The firing pattern of gut muscles might differ from those in intact animals due to the fillet recording methods used.
claims.source: Due to the fillet recording methods we used to gain access of anus sphincter muscles, this firing pattern might differ from those in intact animals.
claims.evidence: This is acknowledged as a potential limitation of the experimental approach.

claims.claim: PDF neurons have been previously shown to promote visceral muscle contractions.
claims.source: The PDF neurons have been previously shown to promote visceral muscle contractions (Talsma et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Light-induced activation of ChR2 in PDF or HGN1 neurons was absent in UAS or Gal4 control larvae and dependent on retinal.
claims.source: This light-induced activation was absent in UAS or Gal4 control larvae and dependent on retinal, which is the chromosphere for ChR2 channels (Figure 2B,C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by control experiments shown in Figure 2B,C.

claims.claim: Both the hindgut and anal sphincter contracted strongly upon blue light stimulation of PDF neurons expressing ChR2.
claims.source: Both the hindgut and anal sphincter contracted strongly (Figure 2D) upon stimulation.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: With ChR2 expression in the HGN1 neurons, the anal sphincter but not hindgut contracted upon blue light stimulation.
claims.source: In contrast, with ChR2 expression in the HGN1 neurons, the anal sphincter but not hindgut contracted upon blue light stimulation of HGN1 neurons (Figure 2D and Video 2).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 2D and Video 2.

claims.claim: The contractions induced by ChR2 activation were absent in larvae with only UAS-ChR2 or larvae fed with regular food without retinal.
claims.source: The contractions were absent in larvae with only UAS-ChR2 or larvae fed with regular food without retinal.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by control experiments.

claims.claim: PDF neurons and HGN1 neurons are required for the normal defecation behavior.
claims.source: These results suggest that the PDF neurons and HGN1 neurons are required for the normal defecation behavior.

results.result: Drosophila larvae exhibit stereotypic defecation cycles with a frequency of 38 seconds at 25°C, involving sequential contractions of the hindgut followed by the anal sphincter that expel feces.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C20, C66, and C85 collectively establish the basic defecation behavior through direct behavioral observations, video recordings (Figure 1B-D, Video 1), and quantitative measurements showing consistent 38-second intervals. The sequential nature of contractions and their functional outcome (feces expulsion) are well-documented with appropriate controls and replicates.

results.result: Two groups of glutamatergic motor neurons (PDF and HGN1) innervate the hindgut and anal sphincter respectively, with their cell bodies in the terminal VNC segments and axons forming synaptic boutons on gut muscles.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C4, C21-C24, C67, C88-C90 are supported by comprehensive anatomical characterization (Figure 1E-M), immunostaining for vGlut demonstrating glutamatergic identity, and high-resolution imaging showing bouton structures. The anatomical evidence is consistent across multiple labeling approaches and clearly demonstrates the innervation patterns.

results.result: Optogenetic activation of PDF or HGN1 neurons expressing ChR2 triggers excitatory junction potentials in gut muscles and induces contractions, with PDF neurons activating both hindgut and anal sphincter while HGN1 neurons specifically activate the anal sphincter.
results.evaluation: Claims C25, C26, C94-C97 are well-supported by electrophysiological recordings (Figure 2B,C) and behavioral observations (Figure 2D, Video 2) with appropriate controls (UAS-ChR2 alone, no retinal). The differential effects of PDF vs HGN1 activation on gut regions are clearly demonstrated and replicated (n=15, p<0.001).

results.result: Silencing PDF neurons increases defecation interval from 38s to 94s, while silencing HGN1 neurons alone has no significant effect; silencing both neuronal groups nearly abolishes hindgut movements.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C30, C98 are supported by functional silencing experiments using Kir2.1 (Figure 3A,B) with statistical significance (p<0.001, one-way ANOVA). The differential effects of silencing each neuronal group and the additive effect of silencing both provide strong evidence for their functional roles, though the interpretation in C99 about pressure forcing open the sphincter remains speculative.

results.result: PDF and HGN1 neurons exhibit rhythmic calcium activity with 38-second periodicity matching the defecation cycle, with HGN1 neurons showing calcium signal propagation from dendrites to soma suggesting they receive periodic excitatory inputs.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C31-C34 are supported by in vivo calcium imaging with GCaMP5 (Figure 4A-D,M, Video 3) showing consistent 38-second intervals across multiple animals (n=7-8). The temporal correlation between neuronal activity and behavior is compelling, though the inference about excitatory inputs (C34) is reasonable but not directly proven.

results.result: PDF and HGN1 neurons have overlapping arborizations in the posterior VNC, show GRASP signal indicating close proximity, and exhibit coordinated sequential firing with PDF neurons activating before HGN1 neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C40 are supported by anatomical imaging (Figure 4E,F, Video 4), GRASP experiments with appropriate controls (Figure 4G, Figure 4—supplement 2), and dual-labeling experiments (Figure 4—supplement 3). The simultaneous calcium imaging (Figure 4H-L, Video 5) clearly demonstrates sequential activation. However, the functional connection (C37) remains inferential from GRASP, which indicates proximity but not definitively synaptic connectivity.

results.result: In dissected VNC preparations, HGN1 neurons display periodic calcium activity with reduced regularity, exhibit clusters of EPSCs indicating excitatory input, and fire bursts of action potentials similar to other Drosophila larval motor neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C104 are supported by ex vivo calcium imaging and electrophysiological recordings (Figure 4—supplement 1A-D) with appropriate citations to similar findings in other motor neurons. The reduced regularity in dissected preparations (C100) is acknowledged as a limitation, which strengthens the interpretation. The electrophysiological characterization provides important validation of the motor neuron identity.

results.result: A single mechanosensitive sensory neuron (ASN) innervates the anal slit with dendrites that surround the entire opening and are stretched when the anus opens, responding with calcium elevation at 38-second intervals matching defecation cycles.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C41-C49, C68, C121 are supported by anatomical characterization (Figure 5A,B), calcium imaging showing responses to anus opening (Figure 5C,D, Video 6), and quantitative analysis (Figure 5E, n=7). The specialized morphology with dendrites surrounding the anal slit and the temporal correlation of calcium responses with mechanical stretch provide strong evidence for mechanosensory function.

results.result: The ASN projects to terminal VNC segments where its axons overlap with PDF and HGN1 dendrites, shows strong asymmetric GRASP signal with PDF neurons, and optogenetic activation of ASN increases EJPs in anal sphincter muscles and triggers PDF/HGN1 neuronal responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C54, C109, C110 are supported by anatomical imaging (Figure 5F), GRASP experiments (Figure 5G, Figure 5—supplement 1), optogenetic activation with electrophysiology (Figure 5H,I, n=14, p<0.001), and mechanical stimulation experiments (Figure 5J, Figure 5—supplement 2). The asymmetric GRASP signal (C52) is consistent with the unilateral cell body position. The convergence of anatomical, functional, and physiological evidence strongly supports sensory feedback to motor neurons.

results.result: Laser ablation of ASN at 48hr AEL completely eliminates the neuron while sparing other PPK neurons, and results in abnormal HGN1 rhythmic firing with increased intervals, indicating ASN provides feedback modulation to motor neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C57 are supported by laser ablation experiments with imaging confirmation of specific ASN elimination (Figure 5K) and calcium imaging showing altered HGN1 activity (Figure 5L). The specificity of ablation and the functional consequence on motor neuron rhythmicity provide strong causal evidence for ASN's role in feedback modulation, though the exact mechanism remains to be determined.

results.result: The TRP channel NOMPC is required for ASN mechanotransduction, as evidenced by increased defecation intervals in nompC mutants, loss of calcium responses in ASN of nompC mutants, and rescue by NOMPC expression, identifying a new role for NOMPC in sensing radial stretch.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C58, C59, C60-C63, C113 are supported by behavioral analysis in mutants (Figure 6A, n=6-7, p<0.001), immunostaining showing NOMPC expression in ASN (Figure 6—supplement 1), calcium imaging in nompC mutants (Figure 6B,C, Video 8), and genetic rescue experiments (Video 9). The convergence of behavioral, expression, functional, and rescue data provides strong evidence for NOMPC's specific role in ASN mechanotransduction.

results.result: The mechanotransduction channels INACTIVE, NANCHUNG, and PIEZO are not required for ASN function, as defecation intervals remain normal in iav, nan, and piezo mutants, and ASN calcium responses are normal in iav mutants.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C10, C64, C65 are supported by behavioral measurements in mutants showing normal defecation intervals (Figure 6A) and calcium imaging in iav mutants showing normal ASN responses (Figure 6C, Video 10, n=9). The negative results with appropriate controls strengthen the specificity of NOMPC's role. However, sample sizes for some mutants are not explicitly stated.

results.result: PDF neurons do not directly synapse with anal sphincter muscles but can trigger sphincter contractions, suggesting functional connections between PDF and HGN1 neurons possibly involving synaptic connections, though multiple neurons may be involved.
results.evaluation: Claims C27, C73, C124 involve inferences about circuit connectivity that are not definitively proven. While C27 is supported by anatomical observations showing PDF axons do not directly innervate the sphincter, the nature of PDF-HGN1 connections (C73, C124) remains uncertain. GRASP indicates proximity but not definitive synaptic connectivity, and the authors appropriately acknowledge alternative possibilities. Additional experiments (e.g., electron microscopy, trans-synaptic tracing) would be needed to definitively establish synaptic connections.

results.result: Gut muscles receive tonic excitatory inputs as measured by electrophysiology, though the firing pattern may differ from intact animals due to the fillet preparation method.
results.evaluation: Claims C91, C92 are supported by electrophysiological recordings (Figure 2A) with appropriate acknowledgment of potential limitations from the dissection method (C92). The authors' transparency about methodological limitations strengthens the interpretation. The tonic input pattern provides baseline characterization, though its physiological relevance to intact behavior is uncertain.

results.result: Robust rhythmic defecation in larvae may facilitate nutrition intake and waste expulsion, while adult flies may require more controllable defecation due to complex environments, with peristaltic hindgut movements potentially generating sufficient pressure to open the sphincter.
results.evaluation: Claims C70, C71, C99, C116, C117 are largely speculative interpretations not directly tested in this study. While C116 and C117 are supported by citations to previous work, C70, C71, and C99 represent reasonable hypotheses but lack direct experimental support. These interpretations are appropriately presented as speculative in the discussion but do not constitute supported results.

results.result: Several open questions remain for future investigation, including whether ASN has dual sensory functions, the mechanism of rhythmic entrainment of motor neurons, the role of PDF neuropeptide, and evolutionary conservation of defecation mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C72, C74, C122, C125-C127, C129 are explicitly stated as open questions or speculative future directions. These are appropriately identified as areas requiring additional investigation and do not represent current findings. They provide valuable context for future work but should not be evaluated as supported results.

results.result: Background knowledge and prior work establish that defecation is essential for survival, Drosophila larvae are useful model organisms, various genes and channels have been previously characterized, and defecation circuits have been studied in other organisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C17, C75-C84, C93, C104, C107, C108, C111, C112, C114, C115, C118-C120, C128 represent background knowledge and prior work supported by appropriate citations. These provide essential context for the current study and are generally well-established facts in the field. The citations appear appropriate and the knowledge claims are standard for the field.

results.result: Anatomical organization of the larval gut and nervous system, including the location of hindgut, anal sphincter, and the positioning of motor neuron cell bodies in terminal VNC segments, enables the experimental approaches used in this study.
results.evaluation: Claims C18, C19, C86, C87, C105, C106 describe anatomical features that are directly demonstrated through imaging (Figure 1A, Figure 1—supplement 1, Figure 4E) or reasonably inferred from neuroanatomical organization (C87). These anatomical descriptions provide essential foundation for the functional studies and are well-supported by the imaging data and citations to previous anatomical work.
